blocks.heading: Choosing a clear representation
blocks.text: Tabulation presents figures in labelled rows and columns. Bar charts compare categories with equally wide separated bars and a common numerical scale. Pie charts show shares of one whole, with sector angles proportional to values. Line graphs can show actual values through time, using ordered time intervals on the horizontal axis and a labelled measure on the vertical axis. Choose the representation that answers the decision: categories are not automatically a time trend. State title, period, units, categories and the relevant total; avoid scales that exaggerate differences. A chart makes information clearer but cannot remove sampling bias or turn preferences into guaranteed demand.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text:
Forty respondents each choose one collection option: workplace 20, shop 15, delivery 5. Draw separated bars at 20, 15 and 5 on a respondent-count axis starting at zero, with collection categories on the horizontal axis. Workplace is most selected in this sample, with half the responses; it is not proof half the whole market will buy.

![Collection preferences](diagrams/collection-bar.png)

blocks.heading: Time-series line graphs
blocks.text: A time-series line graph plots recorded values against ordered time periods. Label both axes and units, choose a consistent scale, plot each point accurately and join consecutive observations in time order. A fall between two periods should be shown rather than replaced with a smooth theory curve. The graph describes the data; it does not explain the cause without more evidence.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text:
Fictional Omi Lunches records annual orders: 2022—40, 2023—60, 2024—55, 2025—80. Plot those years horizontally and number of orders vertically, including the fall from 60 to 55. Overall orders double from 40 to 80, but the path is not a continuous rise. It is not a generic product-life-cycle diagram.

![Annual orders](diagrams/orders-line.png)

blocks.heading: Pie charts
blocks.text: A pie chart represents a whole as proportional sectors. Divide each category count by the total and multiply by 360 degrees for its angle, or by 100 for its percentage. Check that categories form one non-overlapping whole and angles total 360 degrees. Include a title and category key. A pie chart suits shares but makes small differences harder to compare than bars.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text:
Forty respondents select one preferred format: box 12, wrap 18, salad 10. Box is 30% and 108 degrees; wrap is 45% and 162 degrees; salad is 25% and 90 degrees. Angles total 360 degrees. Wrap is the largest share but below half, so it is not a majority preference.

![Format shares](diagrams/format-pie.png)

blocks.heading: Bar charts
blocks.text: A bar chart uses separate bars for distinct categories, with equal widths and a shared scale. Heights show category values; the spacing indicates categories rather than a continuous numerical interval. Label the categories and the measure, give a title and plot the counts accurately. A zero baseline gives a clear comparison of bar lengths. Unlike a pie chart, bars need not describe shares of one whole, although this example does.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text:
A fictional meal survey records box 12 responses, wrap 18 and salad 10, each respondent choosing one format. Draw the bars at 12, 18 and 10. Wrap leads box by six responses and salad by eight, but this sample does not establish the preferences of every potential buyer.

![Format counts](diagrams/format-bar.png)

blocks.heading: Tabulation
blocks.text: Tabulation arranges data into rows and columns with clear headings and units. It helps readers locate exact figures and check totals before constructing a chart. Separate counts from percentages and state the survey base. A table without headings may leave readers unable to distinguish sales value from respondents. Check that category totals fit the stated number of responses, especially if multiple answers were allowed.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text:
A fictional survey of forty people permits one format choice each: box 12, wrap 18, salad 10. Original table:

| Preferred format | Respondents | Share of 40 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Box | 12 | 30% |
| Wrap | 18 | 45% |
| Salad | 10 | 25% |
| Total | 40 | 100% |

The table preserves exact counts and the denominator; it does not describe forty confirmed purchases.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why fictional Iya Goods’ annual sales figures for four named years need an actual time-series graph rather than an unmeasured product-life-cycle curve.

The task concerns recorded values at stated times, so plot those values on labelled time and sales axes, including any fall. A product-life-cycle curve models stages and cannot replace the observations. A bar chart can compare values, but it would not satisfy a specific request to construct a time-series line graph.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Research evidence and a research decision
blocks.text:
Fictional Omi Lunches surveys forty intended local buyers using a neutral single-choice format question: “Which format would you prefer at N$35: box, wrap, salad or would not buy?” All forty choose a format: box 12, wrap 18, salad 10. It also has last year’s sales records. The manager considers treating wrap’s lead as proof of enough demand for a large launch.

a(i) Define market research. [2]
a(ii) State two features needed on a clear bar chart of these results. [2]
b State two reasons to research before a launch. [2]
c Distinguish Omi’s survey from its existing sales records, referring to the questionnaire purpose. [6]
d Evaluate using the charted preference lead as sufficient evidence for a large launch. [8]

a(i) Collecting and analysing information relevant to a market decision. a(ii) Labelled categories and a respondent-count scale. b Reducing uncertainty about needs and guiding a suitable offering. c The neutral question gathers new primary data tailored to format and price. Last year’s records are existing internal secondary information and may describe a different offer. Both can help, but the new survey is not automatically free of sampling or stated-intention limits. d A bar chart shows wrap’s lead clearly; a pie chart shows its 45% share, which is below half. Neither turns forty stated preferences into confirmed sales or establishes launch volume. Use the evidence for a limited trial and investigate demand and cost before a large commitment.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Research evidence and a research decision
blocks.text:
Fictional Omi Lunches surveys forty intended local buyers using a neutral single-choice format question: “Which format would you prefer at N$35: box, wrap, salad or would not buy?” All forty choose a format: box 12, wrap 18, salad 10. It also has last year’s sales records. The manager considers treating wrap’s lead as proof of enough demand for a large launch.

a Draw a labelled bar chart of the three response counts and explain its main finding and limit. [8]
b Evaluate the manager’s large-launch proposal compared with a small trial supported by further suitable research. [12]

a Bars: box 12, wrap 18, salad 10, on a common respondent-count scale beginning at zero, with category labels and a title identifying forty responses. Wrap leads by six over box but does not have a majority.

![Checked format chart](diagrams/format-bar.png)

b Research reduces uncertainty but these are stated choices, not actual purchase commitments. Neutral wording and intended local respondents help relevance, while the small base and one proposed price limit certainty. Existing records offer background but may concern another menu. A large launch could create unsold stock if interest fails to convert. Prefer a small paid-sales trial, track actual purchases and supplement specific missing evidence before scaling. Retain the questionnaire’s price and no-purchase option in further work rather than ask leading questions that force favourable responses.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Research evidence and a research decision
blocks.text:
Fictional Tula Meals surveys forty intended local customers about format at a feasible price using neutral questions. Wrap receives 18 responses, box 12 and salad 10. It considers a small paid-sales trial before committing to a large launch. Historical records concern a different menu.

Evaluate a small trial against a large immediate launch at Tula under the original evidence. Give a concise plan. [12]

Evidence: neutral primary responses from intended buyers; existing records describe another menu. Presentation: bars compare counts and a pie shows wrap at 45%, not a majority. Limitation: intentions do not prove volume of paid demand. Trial: tests purchases at a feasible price while limiting stock risk. Cost: time and smaller initial sales. Judgement: use the trial and review results before a large launch.
